title: The Engineer of Wichita: Cracking Units, Cato, and a Company That Never Went Public
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Austere House on the Arkansas River

stops.name: Wichita, born into the second fortune
stops.date_confidence: attested. Day and month from the Wikipedia article on Charles Koch; the year is fixed independently by Forbes, which gives his age as 90 in August 2026. No hospital or street address was established in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Charles de Ganahl Koch is born in Wichita, second of the four sons of Fred Chase Koch and Mary Clementine Robinson. The town is flat and windy, an aircraft and oil town on the Arkansas River, rich in a way that does not show on the street; ninety years later Forbes will still give it as his address. His father is an engineer who has already made a fortune abroad building oil-cracking units, and who runs the household on a theory: that inherited money ruins a boy unless labor is inserted between him and it.
suggested_refs: Daniel Schulman, Sons of Wichita (2014), on the household and the four brothers

stops.name: Wichita, the dandelions and the manure
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The chores are attested in the Wikipedia article and repeated across the biographical literature, but the starting age of about six is the family's own telling and the year here is an ordering device, not a dated event.
stops.campa: From about the age of six the boy is put to work on the family land: digging dandelions out of the lawn, milking, shoveling manure, mending fence. The money is real and the austerity is deliberate. Fred Koch, who in 1958 will be among the founding members of the John Birch Society, is raising sons against what he believes affluence does to a man, and Charles is the one the method is applied to hardest. Before he finishes high school he will have been sent to eight schools.
suggested_refs: The Koch family land outside Wichita, where the chores were set

stops.name: Culver, the military academy on Lake Maxinkuckee
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Koch's attendance at Culver and the expulsion story rest on the dossier's family-history citation alone; the independently fetched Culver Academies page confirms the school and its location and does not mention him. The year orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Among the schools is Culver Military Academy on the shore of Lake Maxinkuckee in Indiana, an institution of uniforms, cavalry drill, and a chain of command, five hundred miles from Kansas. Family accounts hold that he is expelled from it for drinking on a train. No school record confirms this and no independent source places him at Culver at all; the story survives because the family has told it. He is moved from one institution to the next at his father's decision, eight of them before he finishes school. Whether Culver was among the eight is not something the record settles.
suggested_refs: Culver Academies, 1300 Academy Road, Culver, Marshall County, Indiana
sources: Charles Koch dossier, citing family history

segments.name: Cambridge, and the Training of an Engineer

stops.name: MIT, the general engineering degree
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the degree and year (Wikipedia, 'Charles Koch'; Forbes lists MIT bachelor's and master's degrees). Month is a convention for commencement. Coordinate is the corpus canonical MIT pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: He enters MIT because his father went there and because his father says he will. Fred Koch took a degree in chemical engineering practice from the same institute in 1922. Charles joins Beta Theta Pi, takes the general engineering course, and finds in the coursework something the Kansas fields never offered: a formal method for taking a system apart and seeing what each piece is for. The bachelor of science comes in 1957. He does not leave. Two graduate degrees follow, and the Cambridge years run to seven.
suggested_refs: Fred C. Koch's own MIT degree in chemical engineering practice, 1922

stops.name: MIT, two master's degrees and a disagreement about the date
stops.date_confidence: attested as to both degrees; contested as to the second date. Wikipedia gives the chemical-engineering master's as 1959, the research dossier as 1960, and notes that published profiles disagree. 1959 is used here; 1960 is the recorded variant and is not resolved.
stops.campa: A master of science in nuclear engineering follows in 1958, and a second master's, in chemical engineering, a year later. He is training for reactors and for process plants at the moment when American refining is being rebuilt around continuous catalytic cracking, the technology his father sold to the Soviet Union and to Germany a quarter century before he was born. Nothing in the coursework points toward politics. Sources disagree over whether the second degree was conferred in 1959 or in 1960, and the disagreement is not settled.
suggested_refs: Winkler-Koch cracking units, fifteen built in the Soviet Union 1929 to 1932, the father's business

stops.name: Cambridge, the consulting job at Acorn Park
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Arthur D. Little page lists Koch among notable former employees but gives no dates, so the 1960 to 1961 tenure rests on the dossier alone. Place corrected: the pool said Boston, but ADL left Boston in 1917 for Cambridge and later Acorn Park.
stops.campa: Out of school he takes a post as an engineering and management consultant with Arthur D. Little, at the Acorn Park campus in Cambridge, a firm whose business is hiring engineers to think about other companies' problems. He is twenty-four, salaried, unmarried, two thousand miles from Kansas, and by his own later account he had not planned to leave. He calls it an attractive independent career. The firm's roster of former employees lists his name and no dates at all.
suggested_refs: Arthur D. Little, Acorn Park, Cambridge, Massachusetts
sources: Charles Koch dossier, for the dates

stops.name: Larkspur, the Freedom School in the pines
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Robert LeFevre's school at Larkspur is confirmed for 1956 to 1973 by the fetched Wikipedia article on LeFevre, which does not mention Koch. His attendance and later trusteeship are widely reported elsewhere and rest here on the dossier alone.
stops.campa: Between Cambridge and Wichita he spends time at Robert LeFevre's Freedom School in the pine country south of Denver, a residential seminar in radical libertarian doctrine kept by a man who rejects the state root and branch. The reading is Mises, Hayek, Bastiat, Spooner. Koch becomes a supporter and in time a trustee of the school, which runs at Larkspur from 1956 to 1973. He will spend the next sixty years funding institutions that teach this material.
suggested_refs: Robert LeFevre's Freedom School, later Rampart College, Larkspur, Colorado, 1956 to 1973
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert LeFevre' (school location and dates only)

segments.name: Wichita, the Company and the Father's Name

stops.name: Wichita, the return at twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the return and his age (dossier from Schulman's Sons of Wichita and the company's own history); month is an ordering convention. Headquarters coordinate corrected to the 4111 E 37th St N area at 37.7545, -97.2870.
stops.campa: Fred Koch asks his son to come home, and Charles comes. He is twenty-five. The consulting career ends and he takes over Koch Engineering, a small unit making the internals of distillation towers, alongside the oil-gathering and refining business his father assembled out of several companies with several names. He later says he came back to keep the thing out of other hands, and stayed because the problem of how to run it turned out to be more interesting than any consulting brief.
suggested_refs: Koch Engineering Company, Wichita, maker of distillation-tower internals
sources: Charles Koch dossier, from Schulman, Sons of Wichita

stops.name: Wichita, the presidency, in a year nobody agrees on
stops.date_confidence: contested, and left open. The dossier chronology gives 1966; Wikipedia gives 1967; Forbes says only that he has been chairman since 1967. No fetched source supports 1966. The pool's attested tag on this item is unearned and is demoted here.
stops.campa: Six years after coming home he is president of the family's oil and refining company. The date is contested: one chronology puts it in 1966, another in 1967, and the record that can be checked says only that he has been chairman since 1967. He is thirty-one or thirty-two, running a firm of roughly three hundred people, with Koch Engineering and its distillation-tower internals alongside it. The main business is gathering crude and refining it, and its margins live in measurement and in the price paid at the wellhead.
suggested_refs: Rock Island Oil and Refining Company, one of the predecessor entities

stops.name: Wichita, chairman at thirty-two
stops.date_confidence: attested. Fred Koch's death of a heart attack while duck hunting near Ogden, Utah, on 17 November 1967 is confirmed at the Wikipedia article on Fred C. Koch. No source says whether Charles was on the trip, so the stop is staged at Wichita and not in Utah; the exact hunting site is undocumented.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November Fred Koch dies of a heart attack while duck hunting in Utah. David Koch's account has him calling out praise for a magnificent shot moments before he falls. No source says whether Charles was on that trip, and the exact hunting ground is undocumented. Charles is thirty-two, six years back from Cambridge. He becomes chairman and chief executive of a company of about three hundred employees, and he inherits it whole, with no public shareholders and no outside board to answer to.
suggested_refs: The Bear River duck grounds near Ogden, Utah, where Fred Koch died; his own location, not his son's

stops.name: Wichita, the company takes the dead man's name
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the honorific motive; the predecessor entity is disputed and is deliberately not named in the campa. The dossier says Rock Island Oil and Refining; the Wikipedia article on Koch, Inc. says Wood River Oil and Refining. Both belong to Fred's assemblage.
stops.campa: In the year after the funeral the board renames the company Koch Industries, Inc., in honor of the dead father. What exactly it was called the day before is a matter on which the sources do not agree, because Fred left behind a tangle of entities under several names, and the son's first structural act is to put one surname across the whole of it. He is thirty-three. The name stays on the building in Wichita, and from 2023 the firm styles itself Koch, Inc.
suggested_refs: Koch Industries, Inc., renamed 1968; from 2023 styled Koch, Inc.

stops.name: Rosemount, the fifty percent at Pine Bend
stops.date_confidence: attested. The 35 percent plus Marshall's 15 percent reaching 50 and blocking Union Oil is confirmed at the Wikipedia article on Koch, Inc. Coordinate corrected to the refinery's own coordinate, spanning Rosemount and Inver Grove Heights. Charles Koch's personal presence at the plant is not documented.
stops.campa: On the bluffs south of Saint Paul the Great Northern refinery sits at the top of the continent's crude flow, near enough to Canadian heavy oil to buy it cheap and far enough from the Gulf refiners to sell into the upper Midwest unopposed. Koch holds thirty-five percent. Union Oil moves to take control. Koch combines his stake with the fifteen percent held by the Texas oilman J. Howard Marshall II, reaches fifty, and the takeover dies. Union's stake is bought out afterward. Christopher Leonard will call Pine Bend the core asset of the whole firm.
suggested_refs: Pine Bend Refinery, Rosemount and Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota
Christopher Leonard, Kochland (2019), on Pine Bend as the company's core asset

stops.name: Menlo Park, the Institute for Humane Studies
stops.date_confidence: the institution's 1961 founding by F. A. Harper is attested, as is Koch's later role as chairman emeritus and his $12.4 million of giving from 2008 to 2012. The date here is an ordering device only: no source dates the beginning of his involvement. Coordinate inherited from the corpus pin for IHS at Menlo Park.
stops.campa: F. A. Harper, whom everyone calls Baldy, founded the Institute for Humane Studies at Menlo Park in 1961 to keep classical-liberal scholarship alive at a moment when no university would house it. Koch becomes deeply involved, funds it, and in time sits as chairman emeritus of its board. The Institute does not publish manifestos; it runs fellowships, summer conferences, and a pipeline of graduate students, which is to say it manufactures staff. Between 2008 and 2012 his giving to it comes to twelve point four million dollars.
suggested_refs: Institute for Humane Studies summer conferences, Menlo Park, California, 1970s

stops.name: San Francisco, the founding of Cato
stops.date_confidence: attested: founded January 1977 in San Francisco by Ed Crane, Murray Rothbard and Charles Koch, named at Rothbard's suggestion after Cato's Letters. The dossier's claim of a 1974 predecessor called the Charles Koch Foundation, renamed in 1977, is supported by no reachable source and is dropped. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from murray_rothbard.journey.json.
stops.campa: In San Francisco he puts up the money for a think tank founded with Ed Crane and Murray Rothbard, named at Rothbard's suggestion for Cato's Letters, the English radical pamphlets of the seventeen twenties. Koch supplies the funding, Crane the organization, Rothbard the doctrine. It is the first libertarian institution in America with a serious budget behind it, and the first place where the money and the argument sit in the same room. Within four years the three founders will have broken with each other.
suggested_refs: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon, Cato's Letters (1720-1723), the source of the institute's name
sources: murray_rothbard.journey.json, stop 'San Francisco, the founding of Cato'

stops.name: Wichita, the essay against welfare for the rich
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the essay and the year. The primary text at libertarianism.org returned HTTP 429 on every attempt this session; the quotation is carried through Mother Jones, March 2015, which quotes the sentence in full and links back to the primary.
stops.campa: He publishes a call to arms addressed to the business community, arguing that companies which lobby for subsidies, tariffs, and protective regulation while denouncing welfare have already lost the argument. How discrediting it is, he writes, to request welfare for ourselves while attacking welfare for the poor. He is forty-two. It is the earliest such statement in his own hand, and he makes it from inside a company that takes the mandates and the subsidies too.
stops.quote: Our critics rightfully claim that we want socialism only for the rich.
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, 'The Business Community: Resisting Regulation,' Libertarian Review, 1978, quoted in Mother Jones, March 2015
suggested_refs: Charles Koch, 'The Business Community: Resisting Regulation,' Libertarian Review (1978)
sources: Mother Jones, March 2015, quoting the 1978 essay

stops.name: Wichita, the brother on the ballot
stops.date_confidence: attested as to David Koch's candidacy, his roughly $2.1 million of self-financing, and the ticket's approximately 921,000 votes. Charles's own location on election day is undocumented; the stop is staged at Wichita, where the decision to fund the run was made.
stops.campa: He encourages his brother David to run for vice president on the Libertarian ticket under Ed Clark, in part because campaign-finance law lets a candidate spend without limit on himself. David puts in about two point one million dollars. The ticket takes some nine hundred twenty-one thousand votes, the party's best national result to that date. Charles draws the conclusion that elections are the wrong instrument and turns the money toward institutions instead. In the Federal Election Commission filings the two point one million is recorded as the candidate's own.
suggested_refs: The Clark-Koch Libertarian Party ticket, 1980, and its Federal Election Commission filings

stops.name: Washington, Cato moves east and Rothbard is put out
stops.date_confidence: attested: the relocation from San Francisco to a historic house on Capitol Hill in 1981, and Rothbard's removal by the Crane-controlled board with Koch backing in the same year. The exact Capitol Hill address is not given in the source and the coordinate is approximate.
stops.campa: Cato leaves San Francisco for a historic house on Capitol Hill, three thousand miles closer to the government it exists to argue with. In the same year the board, controlled by Crane with Koch backing, removes Murray Rothbard, after the quarrel over the Clark campaign and over what the money had been for. The doctrine stays and the doctrinaire goes. Rothbard spends the rest of his life denouncing what he calls the Kochtopus, a word that is in circulation from the eighties onward and whose coiner nobody has established.
suggested_refs: murray_rothbard.journey.json, stop 'San Francisco, removed from the board'

stops.name: Fairfax, the hundred million at George Mason
stops.date_confidence: attested via one academic study of the tax filings, which found more than $100 million in twenty-one grants from 1988 to 2016, about 57 percent of his university giving in the period. The date here orders the segment across that span. The honorary doctorate from George Mason is attested and undated.
stops.campa: Across the Potomac in Fairfax, George Mason University becomes the heaviest-funded university node of the whole project: more than a hundred million dollars from his foundation across twenty-one grants between 1988 and 2016, by one study of the tax filings about fifty-seven percent of his university giving in those years. The economics department teaches Austrian and public-choice theory; the law school runs law and economics. In time the university gives him an honorary doctorate.
suggested_refs: Academic tax-filing study of Charles Koch Foundation grants to George Mason University, 1988-2016 (10.1007/s41996-020-00063-0)

stops.name: Arlington, two floors of one building on Washington Boulevard
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the institutions and the shared address at 3434 Washington Boulevard; coordinate corrected from the pool by about 900 metres using OpenStreetMap. Koch's own visits to the building are not documented in any source reviewed.
stops.campa: The Center for the Study of Market Processes begins at Rutgers in the late nineteen seventies under Richard Fink, moves to George Mason University in the eighties, and in 1999 is renamed the Mercatus Center. It shares an Arlington address on Washington Boulevard with the Institute for Humane Studies, brought east from California. One building now holds the graduate pipeline and the regulatory-policy shop of a single funder's project. No plaque on it says so.
suggested_refs: 3434 Washington Boulevard, Arlington, Virginia, shared address of Mercatus and IHS
Jane Mayer, Dark Money (2016), on Richard Fink

stops.name: Wichita, the boardroom challenge
stops.date_confidence: attested. The failed takeover attempt and Bill Koch's removal from employment are recounted in the Tenth Circuit record in Koch v. Koch Industries, Inc., 203 F.3d 1202 (2000), independently fetched.
stops.campa: His younger brother Bill, allied with the eldest brother Frederick and with J. Howard Marshall III, moves to take the board and remove Charles from the head of the company. The attempt fails. Bill is fired the same year. The four sons of a father who thought competition between boys would harden them are now on opposite sides of a proxy fight, and the quarrel passes out of the family's hands. It goes into the federal courts, where it will run until 2001.
suggested_refs: Koch v. Koch Industries, Inc., 203 F.3d 1202 (10th Cir. 2000), No. 98-3223

stops.name: Wichita, the buyout of the dissidents
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Tenth Circuit opinion: roughly 47.8 percent of the company bought from William Koch, Frederick Koch and the Simmons family at about $200 per share, a group total of approximately $1.1 billion.
stops.campa: Koch Industries buys out the dissident shareholders: William Koch, Frederick Koch, and the Simmons family, roughly forty-seven point eight percent of the company. The price is about two hundred dollars a share and the group total is approximately one point one billion dollars. The buyers and the sellers are brothers. Charles and David hold the rest of it between them, and will hold it undiluted by any public market and unreadable from outside for the rest of Charles's working life. The agreement is dated June 1983.
suggested_refs: The June 1983 stock purchase agreement, as recited in 203 F.3d 1202

stops.name: Wichita, the suit over what was not said
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Tenth Circuit opinion. The coordinate is the general Wichita pin for the federal district court, not a surveyed courthouse location.
stops.campa: Two years after taking the money, the bought-out shareholders sue. The claim is that Charles, David, and the company withheld material information before the buyout, above all about the planned expansion of the Pine Bend refinery, and that the shares were therefore worth far more than two hundred dollars each. Damages sought exceed two billion dollars, roughly twice what the whole block of stock fetched. Bill Koch is suing over a price he accepted, on the ground that nobody told him what the refinery was about to become. The case will take thirteen years to reach a jury.
suggested_refs: Koch v. Koch Industries, Inc., the 1985 complaint, as recited in 203 F.3d 1202

stops.name: Wichita, eleven weeks and no damages
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the verdict and its reasoning; the month is an ordering convention. Note that the two Pine Bend trial answers the research pool attributed to Charles Koch are David Koch's testimony in this record, and are therefore narrated here rather than carried as quotations of Charles.
stops.campa: After an eleven-week trial a federal jury finds that the defendants did withhold information about the Pine Bend expansion, and that the omission was not material. The verdict goes to the defendants on every claim and no damages are awarded; the Tenth Circuit affirms. In the trial record it is David, not Charles, who is asked whether he knew in the autumn of 1982 that Pine Bend was heading toward two hundred thousand barrels a day, and who answers that Bernie Paulson had been talking about that number for years.
suggested_refs: Koch v. Koch Industries, Inc., 203 F.3d 1202 (10th Cir. 2000), affirming the verdict

segments.name: The Ledger of Spills and Measurements

stops.name: Lively, the butane in the low ground
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the rupture, the two deaths, and the 1999 verdict. The victims' ages given in the research pool could not be confirmed by any reachable source and are omitted here; the cited UPI archive returned 403. Coordinate corrected: Lively is in Kaufman County, not Rusk, and the pool's pin was about 150 km wrong.
stops.campa: An eight-inch Koch Pipeline liquid-petroleum line, corroded through, ruptures in the fields outside Lively in Kaufman County, southeast of Dallas. Butane pools in the low ground and the smell carries. Two teenagers, Danielle Smalley and Jason Stone, drive a pickup toward it to report the leak, and the vapor ignites. Both are killed. In 1999 a Texas jury finds negligence and malice and returns two hundred ninety-six million dollars against the company.
suggested_refs: CBS News, 'Blood and Oil,' on the Lively rupture and the 1999 verdict

stops.name: Wichita, twenty-four thousand five hundred eighty-seven false claims
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the figures, which come from the False Claims Act opinion at 57 F. Supp. 2d 1122 as cited in the dossier and not independently refetched. The quotation is attested to Charles Koch by CBS News. Court coordinate is the general Wichita pin.
stops.campa: A civil jury finds twenty-four thousand five hundred eighty-seven false claims by Koch Oil in the measurement of crude bought from federal and Native American leases, with roughly five hundred fifty-three thousand dollars in royalty underpayments for the period at issue. The suit was brought under the False Claims Act by his brother Bill. The company's position throughout is that gauging a tank of oil is an inexact business and that the discrepancies run both ways.
stops.quote: There's always a problem of accuracy in the oil field in measurement.
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, testimony on the oil-measurement and royalty litigation, quoted in CBS News, 'Blood and Oil'
suggested_refs: United States ex rel. Precision Co. v. Koch Industries, 57 F. Supp. 2d 1122

stops.name: Houston, thirty million dollars and no defendant
stops.date_confidence: attested. The settlement, the amount, and its status as the largest civil environmental fine then imposed under federal law are confirmed on the EPA enforcement case page, independently fetched. Coordinate is the Houston federal courthouse area.
stops.campa: In a Houston federal court Koch Industries agrees to a thirty million dollar civil penalty, settling allegations of more than three hundred oil spills across six states between 1990 and 1997. It is the largest civil environmental fine imposed on any company under federal law to that date. It is the second week of January in a year that will also bring a ninety-seven count federal indictment against the company in Texas. The penalty is paid. No individual is charged, and the operations that produced three hundred spills go on operating.
suggested_refs: EPA enforcement case page, Koch Industries Inc. oil spills settlement, 13 January 2000

stops.name: Corpus Christi, ninety-seven counts and one plea
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Both Department of Justice releases cited by the dossier are the only sources for the indictment and the plea, and the April 2001 release returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch this session. Refinery coordinate is approximate. Charles Koch is not a named defendant.
stops.campa: A federal grand jury returns a ninety-seven count indictment against Koch Industries, Koch Petroleum Group, and four employees, over benzene emission controls, hazardous waste handling, and false statements at the West Plant refinery on the ship channel. In April 2001 it ends in a plea to a single count of making a false statement about wastewater compliance: ten million dollars in criminal fines and ten million toward local environmental projects. The individual defendants walk.
suggested_refs: Department of Justice releases of 28 September 2000 and 9 April 2001 on the Corpus Christi refinery
sources: Charles Koch dossier, citing justice.gov archive releases (403 on refetch)

segments.name: The Houses and the Undated Honors

stops.name: Indian Wells, the house at The Vintage Club
stops.date_confidence: attested that Indian Wells is a residence (Wikipedia, 'Charles Koch'); the $10 million 1999 purchase and the second house come from the dossier. Coordinate is the Vintage Club area and no exact property is confirmed.
stops.campa: He buys a house at The Vintage Club in the Coachella Valley, reportedly for ten million dollars, and later a second one on the same grounds. It is a golf community at the foot of the Santa Rosa Mountains, where the winter is warm and the gate is closed. He is sixty-three years old and the litigation with his brothers has two years left to run. Wichita is a long way behind him and the company runs without him being in the building. Nothing in the record says how much of the year he spends out here.
suggested_refs: The Vintage Club, Indian Wells, California

stops.name: Aspen, the third address
stops.date_confidence: attested that Aspen is a long-term residence (Wikipedia, 'Charles Koch'); no acquisition date is given anywhere reachable, so the year here orders the segment. General-area coordinate; no property identified.
stops.campa: A third residence, in Aspen, completes the pattern: Wichita for the work, the desert for the winter, the mountains for the summer. What does not move is the company. He never takes the headquarters out of Kansas and never seriously proposes to. Three addresses, and only one of them has an office in it. The campus on East Thirty-seventh Street North in Wichita is where the decisions are made and where they have been made since he came home in 1961. Forbes still lists Wichita as his principal residence at ninety.
suggested_refs: Aspen, Colorado, listed among his residences

stops.name: Topeka, the honorary doctorate at Washburn
stops.date_confidence: the degree is attested in the Wikipedia article on Charles Koch and is undated there and in every other reachable source. The year here is an ordering device only and should not be read as the conferral date. Coordinate corrected to the Washburn campus, about 1.9 km from the pool's value.
stops.campa: Washburn University in Topeka gives him an honorary doctorate. The source that records it does not record the year, and no other reachable source supplies one. Washburn is a municipal university in the state capital, small, and dependent on the legislature and on donors. He holds no earned doctorate; the three MIT degrees stop at the master's, and what he studied there was reactor physics and chemical process design. Two other schools will hand him the same hood, both of those undated as well.
suggested_refs: Washburn University, Topeka, Kansas

stops.name: Manhattan, distinguished citizen of Kansas State
stops.date_confidence: the award is attested in the Wikipedia article on Charles Koch and is undated in every reachable source; the year orders the segment only. Coordinate corrected to the university campus, about 3 km from the pool's value, which fell in downtown Manhattan.
stops.campa: Kansas State University names him a distinguished citizen, on a date nobody records. Kansas honors him because Kansas is where the money stayed: the headquarters in Wichita, the refineries, the pipelines, the foundation grants, a basketball arena, all of it inside a state of under three million people. A privately held company is a different sort of civic fact from a public one, since there are no quarterly filings and no shareholder meeting anyone can attend. The citation, like the doctorates, carries no year.
suggested_refs: Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas

stops.name: Wellesley, the business school gives him a hood
stops.date_confidence: the honorary doctorate from Babson College is attested in the Wikipedia article on Charles Koch and undated in every reachable source; the year is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: Babson College, a business school west of Boston that teaches entrepreneurship and little else, gives him an honorary doctorate, undated in the record like the others. By now he has published The Science of Success, and Good Profit will follow. Both set out Market-Based Management, which is Hayek's knowledge problem applied to a payroll: the attempt to run a firm of a hundred thousand people by internal price signals and distributed decision rights rather than by hierarchy.
stops.quote: At Koch, we believe our emphasis on applying the principles of human progress is foundational to our long-term success. We've seen incredible results when we empower our employees to more fully become all they are capable of being.
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, 'In Their Own Words,' Forbes profile, forbes.com/profile/charles-koch/
suggested_refs: Charles Koch, The Science of Success (2007) and Good Profit (2015)

segments.name: The Network, the Purchases, and the Arena

stops.name: Wichita, the first of the donor seminars
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began hosting these meetings in 2003, and that they were annual at the outset rather than semiannual. The research pool's figure of about seventeen donors is in no reachable source; Mayer's roughly fifteen is attributed to her by name. The venue of the first gathering is undocumented and the stop is staged at Wichita.
stops.campa: Angered by a Republican administration's spending and its steel tariffs, he convenes a small gathering of business owners and philanthropists to discuss what can be done. Jane Mayer's account puts the first meeting at around fifteen people. It becomes an invitation-only seminar, annual and then twice yearly, and by the twenty-tens the donors assembled in those rooms pledge sums comparable to a national party's budget. Attendance is by invitation. The guest list is not published, and neither is the agenda the convener sets.
suggested_refs: Jane Mayer, Dark Money (2016), on the first donor seminar

stops.name: Wichita State University, his name on the arena
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the two dates deliberately split: the $6 million endowment is dated 2002 by the Wikipedia article on Charles Koch, and the renaming to 2003 by the article on the arena itself, which also describes the $25 million renovation of 2002 to 2003. Coordinate from the arena's own article.
stops.campa: A six million dollar endowment given in 2002 helps pay for a twenty-five million dollar renovation of the university's basketball arena at the southeast corner of Twenty-first and Hillside. In 2003 the building is renamed Charles Koch Arena, and the Shockers play there still. It is the only structure anywhere that carries his personal name. The cancer institute at MIT that carries the family name was David's gift, not his, and is routinely credited to them both.
suggested_refs: Charles Koch Arena, Wichita State University, renamed 2003

stops.name: Atlanta, the paper towels
stops.date_confidence: attested as to terms and completion date; the SEC transaction release cited by the dossier returned 403 and the figures are carried from the Wikipedia article on Georgia-Pacific. Charles Koch's personal presence at the Atlanta tower is not documented in any source reviewed.
stops.campa: Koch Industries buys Georgia-Pacific at forty-eight dollars a share, thirteen point two billion in equity and about twenty-one billion including debt, and takes the tower on Peachtree Street along with the pulp mills, the plywood, Brawny, Angel Soft, and Dixie. A company that began by gathering crude oil in Kansas now makes paper towels. The year before it bought INVISTA from DuPont, nylon and spandex; in 2013 it will buy Molex and its electronic connectors.

stops.name: Wichita, suing his own think tank
stops.date_confidence: attested: Niskanen died October 2011, the Kochs filed suit in Kansas in March 2012, and it settled in June 2012. The pool's span of 2011 to 2012 is tightened here. The specific Kansas division is unidentified, so the general Wichita coordinate stands as a placeholder.
stops.campa: William Niskanen, Cato's chairman and one of four shareholders in an institute structured like a private company, dies in October. Charles and David sue in Kansas the following March, arguing that the shareholder agreement requires his stock be offered back rather than passing to his widow. The libertarian press reads it as a takeover of the movement's own house. It settles in June: Ed Crane retires, the board is enlarged, and the shareholder structure that made the suit possible is abolished outright.
suggested_refs: The Cato Institute shareholder agreement, abolished in the June 2012 settlement

stops.name: Wichita, agreeing with a democratic socialist
stops.date_confidence: the Washington Post op-ed of 18 February 2016 is a dossier citation, not refetched. The quotation carried here is from the earlier Wall Street Journal piece of 2 April 2014, reached through a full reprint and corroborated by AEI; the pool's source line for it, a quotation aggregator and a date of circa 2012, was wrong.
stops.campa: In the Washington Post he writes that Bernie Sanders is right about one thing, that the system is rigged and that corporate welfare is what rigs it. He had put the same argument in the Wall Street Journal two years earlier, in a piece headed I'm Fighting to Restore a Free Society, and had conceded there that his own company opposes such favors even when it benefits from them. The billionaire and the democratic socialist share the diagnosis and share nothing that follows from it. The Post piece runs on the eighteenth of February; Koch is eighty.
stops.quote: I believe that cronyism is nothing more than welfare for the rich and powerful, and should be abolished.
stops.quote_source: Charles G. Koch, 'I'm Fighting to Restore a Free Society,' Wall Street Journal, 2 April 2014
suggested_refs: Charles Koch, 'This is the one issue where Bernie Sanders is right,' Washington Post, 18 February 2016
sources: WSJ op-ed of 2 April 2014, via full reprint at joedigenova.org

stops.name: Wichita, the network takes a gentler name
stops.date_confidence: attested: the January 2019 statement of intent and the 20 May 2019 rebrand of the Seminar Network as Stand Together are both confirmed at the Wikipedia article on Stand Together.
stops.campa: In January he says publicly that he is shifting away from partisan politics. In May the Seminar Network is renamed Stand Together and turns its stated attention to poverty, addiction, criminal-justice reform, and education. Critics read the rebrand as laundering. The organization reads it as a return to what the 1978 essay already said. Both readings can be built out of the same set of tax filings. The rebrand is dated the twentieth of May 2019, and he is eighty-three.
suggested_refs: Stand Together, formerly the Seminar Network, rebranded 20 May 2019

stops.name: Wichita, the last of the four brothers inside
stops.date_confidence: attested as to David Koch's death on 23 August 2019 at Southampton, New York, his 2018 retirement for reasons of health, and Julia Koch's inheritance of his 42 percent. Southampton is David's place of death and not a stop of Charles's; the loss is staged at Wichita. The quotation is from the Forbes succession profile of 10 October 2023.
stops.campa: David Koch, who had retired from the company the year before for reasons of health, dies at Southampton. He had been his brother's partner for forty-nine years, the New York half of a Kansas firm, the one who ran for office and put the family name on a cancer institute and a ballet theater. His forty-two percent passes to his widow, Julia. Bill has been out of the company since 1980 and Frederick will die the following February. Charles, at eighty-three, is the only one of Fred Koch's four sons still inside the business.
stops.quote: He had complete integrity, and he wanted to contribute
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch on David Koch, in Matt Durot, 'Billionaire Charles Koch Shares His Secret Plan To Pass On His Fortune And Influence,' Forbes, 10 October 2023
suggested_refs: Frederick R. Koch, the eldest brother, died February 2020

stops.name: Wichita, the sentence in the book
stops.date_confidence: attested. Written by Charles Koch in Believe in People, November 2020, and first reported by the Wall Street Journal on 13 November 2020. wsj.com is unreachable by the research tools, so the wording is confirmed against Business Insider and the Daily Mail of the same date and Salon of 24 November. It is written, not spoken.
stops.campa: He publishes Believe in People with Brian Hooks, and in it he writes that the partisanship he spent forty years funding was a mistake. The Wall Street Journal reports the line first, on the thirteenth of November, and it travels the world inside a day. He names no particular decision, withdraws no particular dollar, and does not dismantle the network the sentence is about. The regret is written down, in a book he is selling, and not said to anybody's face. He is eighty-five.
stops.quote: Boy, did we screw up! What a mess!
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, Believe in People (November 2020), as first reported by the Wall Street Journal, 13 November 2020
suggested_refs: Charles Koch and Brian Hooks, Believe in People: Bottom-Up Solutions for a Top-Down World (2020)
sources: Wall Street Journal, 13 November 2020, via Business Insider and the Daily Mail of the same date

stops.name: Wichita, five point three billion that does not vote
stops.date_confidence: attested by Forbes, refetched 2026-08-23, for the amount, the 2020 to 2022 window, the character of the recipients, and the retention of voting power. The pool's further claims of $4.3 billion to Believe in People and of a record 501(c)(4) donation are in no reachable source and are omitted.
stops.campa: Between 2020 and 2022 he transfers about five point three billion dollars of nonvoting Koch stock to a pair of nonprofits carrying fewer restrictions on lobbying and politics than an ordinary charity. It is nearly a tenth of his forty-two percent stake. He keeps every share that votes, so the money goes and the control does not. One of the two recipients carries the title of the book he published in 2020. Forbes reports the transfers; the second recipient it does not name.
stops.quote: Chase doesn't want my role because he's strong on division of labor by comparative advantage
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, in Matt Durot, 'Billionaire Charles Koch Shares His Secret Plan To Pass On His Fortune And Influence,' Forbes, 10 October 2023

stops.name: Wichita, naming a successor and not retiring
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2 March 2023 leadership announcement, from the company's own release, independently fetched. The October 2023 succession plan for the voting shares is from the Forbes profile of 10 October 2023, not refetched, and is a reconstruction; the quotations are carried against that named article.
stops.campa: Dave Robertson, forty-eight years in the company, is named co-chief executive officer alongside Charles and elected vice chairman; Jim Hannan becomes president and chief operating officer. Koch is eighty-seven and does not retire. In October he tells Forbes that the voting shares will pass to his son Chase, and that Chase and his daughter Elizabeth already hold equal quantities of the nonvoting stock. Of his son he says plainly that he is the better leader of the two.
stops.quote: Dave's the CEO. He is now.

stops.name: Washington, the prize from his own institute
stops.date_confidence: attested as to recipient and year only, from the Wikipedia articles on the Cato Institute and on the Milton Friedman Prize. Neither gives a ceremony date, a venue, or the protest interruption the research pool reported, and cato.org returns 403 to the research tools; the pool's date of 1 May 2025 and the protest are therefore not stated. Coordinate is Cato's headquarters at 1000 Massachusetts Avenue NW.
stops.campa: Forty-eight years after he paid for its founding, the Cato Institute awards him the Milton Friedman Prize for Advancing Liberty, a biennial honor of two hundred fifty thousand dollars whose previous recipient was the imprisoned Hong Kong publisher Jimmy Lai. The house on Massachusetts Avenue has been Cato's since 1993. Ed Crane, who ran the place for thirty-five years, left it in the 2012 settlement of Koch's suit over the shareholder agreement. No source reachable here gives the date of the ceremony, the venue, or who spoke.

stops.name: Wichita, ninety years old and still chairman
stops.date_confidence: attested. Forbes, refetched 2026-08-23, gives the net worth as $73.8 billion and the age as 90. The May 2026 book with Chase Koch is a dossier chronology item and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Forbes puts the estimate at seventy-three point eight billion dollars and the age at ninety. He is still chairman. There is no tomb to visit and no statue: the man is alive, in the city he was born in, inside the company that carries his father's name, and the monuments are an arena, a foundation, and a university economics department. Two of his three brothers are dead, and the company has never sold a share to the public. In May he published a book of principles written with his son.
stops.quote: Let's say I get hit by a bus tomorrow. What's in place will be the immediate succession
stops.quote_source: Charles Koch, in Matt Durot, 'Billionaire Charles Koch Shares His Secret Plan To Pass On His Fortune And Influence,' Forbes, 10 October 2023
